title: The first case: the object form
goal: Face the first of four cases: the form a noun takes when it's on the receiving end of an action — and know exactly when the ending changes and when it doesn't.
bekal: change a noun from its dictionary form to its object form
recognize prepositions that always take þolfall, especially *um*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Göngutúr um miðbæinn
dialogs.intro: Late afternoon in downtown Reykjavík. Anna points out the Hallgrímskirkja church towering at the end of the street, and Búdí asks about everything he sees.

lines.id: Do you see the church over there?

lines.speaker: Búdí:
lines.text: Já, ég sé hana. Hún er mjög stór.
lines.id: Yes, I see it. It's very big.
lines.literal: yes, I see her. she is very big.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: It's called Hallgrímskirkja. Do you know Hallgrímur?

lines.text: Hann var skáld. Allir Íslendingar lesa sálmana hans.

notes: **A noun changes form when it's on the receiving end of an action.** *Kirkjan* (the church) → *Ég sé **kirkjuna***. *Báturinn* (the boat) → *Ég sé **bátinn***. This changed form is called **þolfall** (the accusative), and it's the first of the four cases you'll learn.

**English has almost lost this** — only pronouns still do it (*I/me*, *she/her*, *we/us*), while "I see the church" and "the church is big" use exactly the same noun. So think of Icelandic nouns as behaving like English pronouns, and look for the pattern in the endings — there turn out to be only a few.

**Pronouns change too**: *hann* stays *hann*, but *hún* becomes *hana*, *ég* becomes *mig*, *þú* becomes *þig*. Note *ég sé **hana*** for the church — since *kirkja* is kvenkyn, its pronoun is *hún*, and as an object it becomes *hana*.

**Um is always followed by þolfall, no exceptions.** *Sögur **um víkinga***, *bók **um Ísland***, *tala **um veðrið***. It's one of the few prepositions that never switches case, so it's the safest place to start practicing.
**Ég ætla að taka mynd — the intention form.** *Ætla að* + infinitive means "intend to, be going to". It's one of the two ways Icelandic talks about the future, and it's covered in full in Unit 18.

**Hallgrímskirkja and Hallgrímur Pétursson.** Iceland's tallest church is named after the 17th-century poet who wrote the *Passíusálmar*, fifty hymns still read on the radio every Easter. The church's name is itself a grammar lesson: *Hallgríms* is the possessive form of *Hallgrímur*.

grammars.title: Þolfall — how the endings change
body: The change depends on the noun's gender, and only **karlkyn and kvenkyn** really change. Hvorugkyn stays put — a free gift.
after: Three rules cover almost everything: **kk -ur/-ll/-nn lose their ending**, **kvk -a becomes -u**, and **hk doesn't change at all**. Kvenkyn words with no ending don't change in their bare form either.
Watch the forms with the article: *bókin* → *bókina*, *kirkjan* → *kirkjuna*, *bíllinn* → *bílinn*, *húsið* → *húsið* (unchanged).

⚠️ Since hvorugkyn forms are identical in nefnifall and þolfall, a sentence like *barnið sér húsið* can't be decoded from the endings alone — **word order** decides who sees what. Icelandic is not a free-word-order language.

grammars.title: Pronouns in the object form
body: Eight forms, and some of them look very different from the subject form. Learn them in pairs: *ég – mig*, *þú – þig* — just like English *I – me*.
after: ⚠️ Remember that *ekki* jumps behind an object pronoun: *Ég þekki hann **ekki***, not *ég þekki ekki hann*. This rule came up in Unit 2, and now the reason is clear.
Since things have genders too, you'll often use *hana* and *hann* for objects: *Sérðu bókina? — Já, ég sé **hana**.* ("Do you see the book? — Yes, I see *her*" = it.)

blocks.text: The verbs below are almost always followed by þolfall. Practice each one with a noun from Unit 3, and the object form will stick without memorizing tables.
Some Icelandic prepositions switch case depending on their meaning — that's Unit 11. But the four below **always** take þolfall, whatever the situation.

blocks.title: A really fast way to practice
items: Take ten nouns you already know and say each one twice: once as the subject, once as the object. *Bókin er ný — ég les bókina.* *Bíllinn er stór — ég sé bílinn.*
Pairs like these stick much faster than tables, because what you're learning isn't the form but **the switch**.
